newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian freedom anniversary hit by market blues.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian freedom anniversary hit by market blues.

text.p: Indonesia's booming economy has been hurt by a weakening currency and a falling stock market in the run up to this weekend's 52nd anniversary of independence.

President Suharto, in power for more than three decades and widely acknowledged as the architect of the country's rapid growth, will deliver an annual state-of-the-nation address on independence day eve on Saturday, but analysts say they do not expect him to refer to the economy's current troubles.

The currency, the rupiah, dropped to a historic low against the dollar on Wednesday, a fall of more than 10 percent since the beginning of the year, and the stock market index was trading about 10 percent below the historic high it reached only last month.

Also worrying are the prospects of an extended drought this year because of the dreaded El Nino, the name given to a warm water current which disturbs weather patterns in Pacific Rim nations and is likely to peak in December.

Still, economists say, the 52nd anniversary celebrations on Sunday should be an occasion to mark the great strides the economy of the world's fourth-most populous nation has made since independence in 1945.

"Indonesia has achieved extraordinary success," said former cabinet minister and economist Frans Seda, noting that the country's per capita income had risen to above $1,000 from $50 in the past three decades.

Emerging from centuries of Dutch colonial rule in the aftermath of World War II and an economically disastrous experiment with socialism under founding president Sukarno, Indonesia has moved from near-total poverty to being one of the fastest growing nations in booming Southeast Asia.
Economic growth has clipped along at seven percent per annum or over for the past decade and the government has projected growth of 7.1 percent in 1997-98 (April-March).
It is the only Asian member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries and its oil reserves have kept the country's trade balance in the black for more than two decades.
But Seda said that while there had been success, there had also been some mishaps resulting from the economic achievements.

He said Indonesia had gone through a structural change from an agrarian state to an industrialised nation, with all the attendant social implications, and also a switch to a private sector-led market economy from a co-operative economy.
"This has had a radical social impact which has not been handled properly because it was covered by optimism due to positive results of our development," Seda said.
"We have seen many small explosions because of political and social discontent and they are getting more widespread and violent," the former minister said.

An example was the Jakarta riots in July 1996, which overshadowed last year's independence day celebrations. Mobs angry at the perceived high-handedness of the government towards a minority party rampaged through the capital's streets for hours, burning buildings and vehicles.
At least five people were killed.

Violence also marred the campaign for the May 1997 general elections and political analysts said the perpetrators were mainly urban youth who appeared to have been left behind by the country's speedy growth.

But after the ruling Golkar party romped home to victory, the economy appeared to be headed for a rosy future. Economists said the only real risk on the horizon was how long Suharto, 76, would continue at the helm.
But the contagion effect of regional currency weakness over the past month has taken a heavy toll on the rupiah, and by extension, the stock market.

Although the central bank has taken measures to contain the situation by raising interest rates, an immediate rebound is not in sight. The stock market, capitalised at about $95 billion, has suffered from the rupiah's turbulence.

To add to the country's economic woes, the Central Bureau of Statistics has said inflation might not be kept under the government target of six percent this year if the current drought in rice-growing areas continues.

But economists said the currency impact on economic growth was likely to be muted, although the trade surplus could narrow because of capital goods imports. They have also said that Indonesia's economic fundamentals are strong enough to overcome minor pitfalls.
The World Bank has said if Indonesia were to average 7.5 percent growth per annum through 2005, income per capita would more than double to $2,300.
